newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia deputies mark late Brezhnev's 90th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Russia deputies mark late Brezhnev's 90th birthday.

text.p: Russian deputies nostalgic for the old Soviet Union on Thursday marked what would have been the 90th birthday of the late Leonid Brezhnev, leader of the communist superpower for 18 years till his death in 1982.

Communist and nationalist lawmakers hailed Brezhnev's reign as a golden age of low prices and political stability when Moscow held sway across half of Europe and still ruled a vast multi-ethnic empire.

Brezhnev, the bushy-eyebrowed apparatchik whose rule is now commonly known in Russia as the "stagnation years", took the helm in 1964 after ousting Nikita Khruschev. He died in November 1982 at the age of 75.

Interfax news agency quoted Alexei Mitrofanov of the ultra-nationalist Liberal Democratic Party as saying that the Soviet Union under Brezhnev achieved "its greatest economic ascent by many indicators".

"Brezhnev's service lay in preserving and extending the military-political and economic power of the country, allowing it to exert effective influence over the direction of European and world politics," it quoted Mitrofanov as saying.
Mitrofanov was chairing a meeting of the State Duma's (lower house of parliament) geopolitical committee, which was also attended by some of Brezhnev's old comrades.
The gathering discussed the merits of the so-called "Brezhnev Doctrine" that upheld Moscow's right to intervene in other Eastern bloc countries to defend socialism.
As General Secretary of the Communist Party, Brezhnev authorised the Soviet intervention in Czechoslovakia in 1968 to suppress attempts there to liberalise the communist regime.
He also sent Soviet troops into Afghanistan in 1979 to boost its pro-Moscow rulers, earning international opprobrium and triggering a big chill in East-West relations.
"Brezhnev's conservatism was much more practical than (former Soviet President Mikhail) Gorbachev's castles in the air," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Mitrofanov as saying.
Gorbachev's policy of openness preceded the final collapse of the Soviet Union in December 1991.
